name: Fatima Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal lineworker shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at the electricity company depot, check the truck with the crew, and take the day’s build or repair order. I like the moment we bring a dark street back, and I still test the line myself before anyone touches it. At home my partner and I have two school-age children and a mortgage, so callout nights have to be worth the missed supper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the useful part is faster paperwork, not some grand replacement of lineworkers. I already use AI most days to turn my rough site notes into a clear report, then check every pole number before filing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings cover more than six months and my pay is high for this job, so I am not guarding every hour in fear. I would still be annoyed if a manager mistook a smooth paragraph for proof that a line is safe. A neat AI report will never make a loose power line safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same repair shifts and compare AI drafted reports with my notebook before sending them. During the first year I would show my apprentice the exact checks I use, especially the pole number and isolation record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, to be honest. A small improvement to forms gives me more time with the family, provided the crew keeps responsibility for the actual repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the mistake you most often catch in a drafted report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sometimes puts the right fault on the wrong pole number when two poles share a road name. I make my apprentice point to the number in the field notebook before the report goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new tool in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the company already supplies the report tool and the truck kit. I would keep our family savings for repairs to the house and the usual mortgage payment.

say: I **use** AI for report wording but still verify pole numbers and isolation records.
**Lineworkers** keep physical responsibility even when routine forms become quicker.
think: My **high** pay and long savings cushion make a small software shift manageable.
A **polished** report could mislead a manager about whether a line is actually safe.
do: **Keep** my repair rota and compare each drafted report with my field notebook.
**Show** my apprentice how to check pole numbers and isolation records.
feel: **Calm** about pay and pleased if forms take less family time.
S0.quote: A neat AI report will never make a loose power line safe.
fieldNote: She **already** uses AI daily for notes but insists on physical checks before submission.
**Strong** savings and higher wages keep ordinary family bills from driving immediate worry.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and verify each drafted report against field notes
Show apprentice how to verify AI reports during regular shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that AI scheduling could stop crews driving in circles, and that is worth trying. I would also say the person on the pole must be allowed to correct a bad work order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My line repairs are mainly hands-on, so I expect dispatch and purchasing desks to change first. If quicker planning strips away callout overtime, that would sting, though our savings give us time to adjust. I will test a route on a screen, then test its gate with the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run the new scheduling tool alongside our usual route for a month and record the missed access points. In the first year I would ask the supervisor for a written explanation of any overtime change, then put half of any remaining callout premium toward the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious, with a bit of concern about the extra pay. I can test a tool without pretending every suggestion it makes is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a missed access point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A schedule may put a truck at the front of a property when the gate for line equipment is on the service lane. I would log the detour and its minutes, not just complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if overtime really dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first see the new monthly amount and our mortgage statement. We have more than six months saved, so I would adjust optional weekend spending before I looked for another employer.

say: I would **trial** scheduling AI if crews can correct its work orders.
The **field** team should record actual travel times before targets change.
think: **Dispatch** and purchasing may shrink earlier than physical line repair work.
**Losing** callout premiums would reduce our cushion building, even with strong savings already.
do: **Compare** new route suggestions with truck access for one month.
**Request** a written overtime explanation if the company changes the callout rota.
**Pay** extra on the mortgage from half of any remaining callout premium.
feel: **Curious** about useful routing, with concern over possible overtime loss.
S1.quote: I will test a route on a screen, then test its gate with the truck.
fieldNote: Her **daily** AI use makes a controlled routing trial plausible without trusting it blindly.
She **links** household impact to actual overtime changes and keeps the mortgage in view.

steps.text: Test AI route suggestions against truck access for one month
Pay half of remaining callout premiums toward mortgage if premiums continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 can redraw dispatch quickly, but capable climbing robots come nearer 2031. I would volunteer to evaluate them only if our electricity company pays the crew and records real faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot reaching live lines in three years could eventually take the callouts that made this a higher paid job. Plenty of other electricity companies are nearby, and our savings give me room to move, but I do not want to gamble away the mortgage. A robot’s first mistake on a power line should happen in a paid trial, not above someone’s house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask for a paid place on the robot field trial and practice checking its proposed isolation sequence against our manual procedure. In the first year after 2028, I would move a fresh two hundred from each pay packet into savings and compare paid lineworker posts at nearby firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not stuck. I would rather be the worker finding a robot’s fault than the customer finding it after the lights go out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop a field trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robot failed to identify an isolated span or reached across a marked boundary, I would stop the test immediately. A paid trial is still a safety job, not a show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take another company’s offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The offer would need real field work, comparable pay and training on any new equipment. A vacancy notice alone would not make me quit this electricity company.

say: I would **join** paid field trials before robots work on live lines.
A **robot’s** isolation sequence must be checked against the crew’s procedure.
think: **Capable** robots around 2031 could erode callout pay even after thinking AI changes dispatch in 2028.
**Nearby** jobs and strong savings give choices, but the mortgage rules out a blind leap.
do: **Seek** a paid place on the company robot field trial this year.
**Save** two hundred extra from each pay packet after 2028.
**Compare** nearby paid lineworker posts before considering any move.
feel: **Anxious** about callout pay, yet willing to learn through paid testing.
S2.quote: A robot’s first mistake on a power line should happen in a paid trial, not above someone’s house.
fieldNote: She would **volunteer** early, reflecting high adaptability, but makes pay and fault recording explicit.
The **mortgage** and children keep a strong financial cushion from becoming reckless confidence.

steps.text: Join company robot field trial this year if crew is paid
Save two hundred extra from each pay packet after 2028
Compare nearby paid lineworker posts after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that five years before thinking AI and roughly eight before line robots is enough time to build a better apprenticeship. A capable machine should be taught with workers watching real weather and damaged hardware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2034 our children will be older, but the mortgage will still need paying unless our extra payments hold. I could become a paid equipment trainer if a real vacancy opens, though I would not leave field pay for an impressive title. An apprentice should be paid to find the wrong robot instruction before a line crew ever follows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the training manager this year for the assessor course requirements and the trainer pay band. If the company funds the course and posts a trainer vacancy at comparable pay, I would complete it before 2031 and apply when the post opens; otherwise I would keep line shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More hopeful than in the fast picture. I like being paid to learn a tool and pass on what my apprenticeship taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you include in an apprentice lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would give the apprentice a wrong robot work order and ask them to find the danger before any climb. They need to learn that the line in front of them outranks a smooth instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you decide whether the trainer pay is enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would compare the actual salary and hours against our mortgage and school costs. If it is lower than we can carry, I stay with the repairs.

say: A **longer** runway lets experienced crews shape robot training for apprentices.
I would **support** machines tested on real faults and weather.
think: A **paid** trainer role might fit when the children are older, if pay remains comparable.
The **mortgage** still makes a title without a funded vacancy unattractive.
do: **Request** assessor requirements and trainer pay band from the company this year.
**Complete** funded assessor course before 2031 if comparable trainer vacancy is posted.
**Apply** for the posted trainer role only if its pay covers our household costs.
feel: **Hopeful** about paid learning with time to test actual offers.
S3.quote: An apprentice should be paid to find the wrong robot instruction before a line crew ever follows it.
fieldNote: She **sees** a route from field skill to teaching, grounded in a funded course and genuine vacancy.
Her **family** budget, rather than enthusiasm alone, determines whether a trainer move works.

steps.text: Complete funded assessor course before 2031 if comparable trainer vacancy is posted
Apply for posted trainer role if pay covers mortgage and school costs
Keep line shifts if funded course or suitable vacancy is absent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade before thinking AI in 2036, then robots around 2039, lets a good lineworker build another craft. I would learn to inspect robot repairs and keep the human fault checks in the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three I may want fewer night callouts, and our mortgage could be smaller if earnings hold. I would still want paid work; I am not assuming a pension date or a guaranteed inspection position. Ten years gives me time to inspect what a line robot fixes, not just admire what it can lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the company what qualification a robot repair inspector would need and set a household savings target from my current higher pay. If a recognised inspection course becomes available on paid time, I would take it before 2036; I would apply for an inspection opening only after seeing its salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough to plan without hurrying the children or my partner. A decade lets me judge the machines by repairs they have actually completed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What household savings target would you set?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put one hundred fifty a month from normal wages into a new repair-and-training account, then review it with my partner each year. The existing emergency savings would stay for family needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an inspection opening acceptable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay would need to cover the remaining mortgage and the work would have to include real field checks. I would not trade line shifts for a desk title with no power to stop a faulty repair.

say: A **decade** permits lineworkers to develop robot repair inspection skills before hands-on deployment.
I would **keep** human field checks in the inspection process.
think: At **fifty-three**, fewer night callouts may appeal if an actual paid inspection job exists.
I **cannot** assume the mortgage or future qualifications will settle themselves.
do: **Save** one hundred fifty monthly from current wages for training and home repairs.
**Take** a recognised inspection course before 2036 if offered on paid time.
**Apply** for a field inspection opening only after checking its salary and authority.
feel: **Calm** with time to judge real repairs and keep household choices open.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me time to inspect what a line robot fixes, not just admire what it can lift.
fieldNote: Her **future** plan pairs fresh saving with conditional paid study and a real inspection offer.
She **rejects** automatic retirement and keeps the household mortgage in the decision.

steps.text: Save one hundred fifty monthly from wages into repair-and-training account
Take recognised inspection course before 2036 if offered on paid time
Apply for field inspector opening if salary covers mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots able to climb by around 2031 could cut the paid callouts before a family can adjust its mortgage. Paid trials with real fault records would help, and so would clear offers for training or other line jobs. I can learn a new machine faster than I can undo a careless repair.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the apprentices still get to learn a real fault when a machine handles the easy ones. My certificate and apprenticeship mattered because an older worker let me make safe decisions under supervision. The next crew needs the same chance.

headlineQuote: I can learn a new machine faster than I can undo a careless repair.
portrait: **Fatima** is a forty-three-year-old electricity company lineworker who uses AI daily for reports and checks every pole number against field notes.
Her **apprenticeship** and family duties shape a practical belief in paid work, competent crews and household responsibility.
**Higher** pay, strong savings and nearby employers give her options, while two school-age children and a mortgage keep pay central.
She **volunteers** for paid robot trials under fast AGI and considers training or inspection roles only with funded courses and real offers.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring capable line robots around 2031 and cut well-paid callouts before the mortgage can adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** field trials with real fault records, plus clear training and lineworker offers, would help her judge the move.
